kernelIdea: S × T is the set of ordered pairs (s,t) with s ∈ S and t ∈ T. Order matters, so S × T ≠ T × S in general. Anything × ∅ is ∅. Products interact cleanly with intersection.

kernels.l1: Pick one from here and one from there. Every pairing is its own thing.
kernels.l2: If you pick one thing from each of two groups, you get a pair. Draw a grid and every square is one pair. The number of pairs is the two counts multiplied.
kernels.l3: S × T is the set of all ordered pairs whose first slot comes from S and whose second comes from T. The slots have different jobs, so (a, b) and (b, a) are different objects.
kernels.l4: S × T = {(s,t) | s ∈ S and t ∈ T}. Order matters, so S × T ≠ T × S in general, and S × ∅ = ∅ because there is no second coordinate to choose.
kernels.l5: A product set has ordered pairs as elements, so an arbitrary element must be named (x, y) immediately; equality of pairs means equality in each coordinate.
kernels.l6: S × T is the set of ordered pairs; its defining property is that (a,b) = (c,d) iff a = c and b = d, which is what makes coordinates well defined.
kernels.l7: S × T consists of ordered pairs with first coordinate in S and second in T; the defining property is coordinatewise equality, order matters, and any product with ∅ is empty.
kernels.l8: The cartesian product is characterised up to isomorphism by its projections and the universal property of the categorical product; relations and functions are then defined as subsets of it.
